contentHtml:
Siddhart Dhote, Senior Associate, Data Analyst, Indian School of Development Management, highlights the growing differences in NCD prevalence across Indian states and why the social sector, community organisations and policymakers must work together to ensure continuity of care

India is in the middle of a health transition, and the latest NFHS-6 data offers a glimpse of the future. From 2019-21 to 2023-24, the proportion of men and women with high blood sugar levels increased in 29 and 31 states and UTs, respectively. This tells us the Non-communicable Disease (NCD) burden is not a regional story or an urban elite problem. It is happening across the country, at different speeds and in different directions. That variation is precisely the roadmap for action.

The geographic context elevates this finding. An analysis of obesity against blood sugar across Indian states reveals that different states are at different points in the same journey. What Kerala and Tamil Nadu look like today is what Bihar and Assam could look like in a decade if the trajectory holds. In this respect, the southern states are a forecast for the rest of the country.

This matters significantly for how we plan health interventions. A state that is earlier in the transition does not need the same intervention mix as one already grappling with high obesity and rising blood sugar. It needs investment now in the infrastructure, workforce, and community relationships that will be required when the burden arrives.

India is already undertaking steps to address its NCD burden under the National Health Policy 2017 (NHP 2017), by expanding screening at Health and Wellness Centres, making generic medicines more accessible through Jan Aushadhi stores, and broadening ASHA workers’ roles beyond maternal and child health. But chronic disease management requires something more sustained: ongoing engagement over years instead of one-time programs. It requires behaviour change around diet, activity, and medication adherence, as well as health workers who build continuous relationships with households.

This is where the social sector has a critical role to play, as a coordinator of effort. Governments can build facilities and train workers; researchers can map the burden; and philanthropists can fund innovation. But closing the gap between a service that exists and a person who uses it (and keeps using it, for years) requires all of these working in the same direction. It requires community organisations that have earned household trust, program designers who start from behaviour rather than infrastructure, and funders willing to support the slow, unglamorous work of sustained engagement.

The challenge is not only to expand services, but to redesign the institutions that make chronic care continuous, trusted, and measurable. That means strengthening primary care capacity, creating reliable referral pathways, aligning incentives for long-term follow-up, and building data systems that can track risk, treatment, and adherence over time.

NHP 2017 set the right direction. NFHS-6 tells us where we are on that road, and how much of it still lies ahead. The data suggests that India’s response cannot rely on clinical services alone, but must be organised as a coordinated ecosystem in which governments, health workers, community organisations, researchers, and funders each play distinct roles. India needs to build the organisational and social infrastructure needed to sustain that response over years, not months.

The data on Kerala and Tamil Nadu should not be viewed as exceptions; it is an early sign for policymakers. States that are earlier in the transition, such as the eastern and northeastern states, have a narrow window to build the capabilities, trust, and delivery systems that chronic disease management will require later. They can use this lead time to invest in the kind of community-embedded, regionally designed health infrastructure and programs that southern states are now building.

How India uses this lead time will determine whether the country enters the next phase of its health transition prepared or is forced to build capacity under far greater pressure.
